sources.title: "The Lives of Andrew Carnegie" (Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History)
History.com and Britannica's accounts of the 1892 Homestead Strike

achievement_drive.rationale: Rose from a $2.50-a-week telegraph messenger at age 14 to superintendent of the Pennsylvania Railroad's Pittsburgh division by age 24, then built one of the largest steel enterprises in the world -- an extreme, quantified, rapid career trajectory documented across multiple independent sources.

impact_motivation.rationale: Personally funded roughly 2,500 public libraries worldwide (1,679 in the US alone) and gave away roughly 90% of his fortune, over $350 million, during his own lifetime, with an explicit, articulated philosophy favoring institutions that "help people help themselves" over direct handouts -- a specific, sustained, quantified, strategically-designed giving program.

independent_thinking.rationale: Published "Gospel of Wealth" (1889), articulating the unusual, explicit position that the wealthy are merely "trustees" of their fortune with a moral obligation to give it away during their own lifetime rather than to heirs -- a genuinely counter-cultural stance for a man of his era and class, published years before most of his own giving occurred.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: Personally authorized his operations manager, Henry Clay Frick, to break the steelworkers' union at the Homestead plant ahead of the workers' contract expiration in 1892, a decision that led directly to a lockout of 3,800 workers and a violent confrontation in which 12 people were killed, followed by a documented multi-year reduction in wages and increase in working hours for the remaining workforce -- scored as a real, high-stakes, harmful documented consequence of a deliberate business decision, not framed as a positive trait.

resourcefulness.rationale: Two independent documented instances: taught himself telegraph operation on his own initiative, which directly led to his first major promotion, and sustained his entire education through a philanthropically-provided library for working boys rather than formal schooling.
